summaries.example: Imagine you are in a room with an unlocked door. You can leave, or you can stay, depending on what you decide. Locke would call you free about leaving because you have both choices available. If the door were locked, you might still want to leave, but you would not be free to leave.
summaries.summary: John Locke asks what it means for a person to be free. He says freedom is a power to do something or not do it according to the mind’s direction. This is different from merely wanting something. A person may want to leave a locked room but lack the freedom to leave. Locke also separates voluntary action from freedom: an action can follow a person’s choice while a barrier still prevents other choices. He says the will is a power of the mind, not a separate person that can itself be free. In his later account, the will directs the body or thoughts, while uneasiness—such as pain, worry, or a felt lack—usually pushes it toward action. Importantly, people can sometimes pause a desire, examine it, and consider whether it leads toward lasting happiness. Locke uses this power to explain how people can be responsible for choices, even though their feelings influence them. The entry also explains why many readers see Locke as close to compatibilism: he treats freedom as compatible with causes, as long as a person still has the ability to act or not act as the person decides.
key_ideas: Locke says freedom is mainly about whether people can act or stay still as their minds direct.
An action can be voluntary even when a person cannot really do anything else. For example, someone locked in a room may choose to stay.
The will is not itself a free person. It is a power of the mind, so asking whether the will is free mixes up two different kinds of things.
Locke first connected the will with what seems best, but later said that uneasiness usually moves us to choose.
People can sometimes pause a desire and think before acting. Locke connects this ability with responsibility.
Locke’s view suggests that being caused to act is not automatically the same as being forced. What matters is whether outside barriers remove the ability to act as one decides.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke’s ideas help us tell apart wanting, choosing, acting, and being able to act. These differences matter when we decide whether someone acted freely or was forced. They also help explain why pausing before acting can be important: it gives us a chance to examine our desires instead of simply following the strongest feeling.

important_terms.definition: The ability of a person to do something or not do it according to what the person’s mind directs.
A mental power that gives directions to the body or mind, such as telling your hand to move.
A mental act of directing yourself to do something or to stop doing it.
A feeling of discomfort, pain, or worry that pushes someone toward a change.
Choosing to pause a desire so you can think about whether following it is wise.

questions_to_think_about: Can you be free to choose if you cannot carry out what you choose?
When have you paused before doing something you wanted to do?
Is staying still always a choice?
Does a strong feeling make a decision less free?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is sitting quietly and considers whether to begin a difficult assignment. The assignment is a future action, so the student may suspend the desire to avoid it and examine its consequences. By contrast, if the student is already walking and is asked to stop immediately, Locke’s later discussion suggests that continuing or stopping the ongoing process requires willing one way or the other. The two situations raise different questions about freedom in respect of willing.
summaries.summary: Locke’s theory of freedom begins with a distinction between actions and forbearances. His discussion supports a relatively deflationary account: bodily motions and mental operations count as actions, while forbearances are forms of not acting or resting. The will is a power belonging to an agent. In Locke’s later formulation, it directs the body or mind through thought, and volition is the exercise of that directive power. An action is voluntary when it is caused in the appropriate way by a volition concerning that action. Freedom is different. An agent is free with respect to an action when the agent has the power to perform it if willing and the power to refrain if willing not to perform it. Thus, a person in a locked room may voluntarily remain because of a choice, yet lack the freedom to leave; conversely, a movement caused by another person may be involuntary even when the agent could have moved or refrained. Locke rejects the literal question “Is the will free?” as a category mistake, since a power is not the sort of thing that possesses powers. He replaces it with questions about freedom in respect of willing and freedom to will. His account changes across editions. He first says the apparent greater good determines the will, then argues that uneasiness usually does so. The power to suspend desire allows an agent to delay action, examine competing goods, and avoid blindly following an impulse. Interpreters disagree about how this fits Locke’s claims concerning willing, but the entry presents a reading on which his revisions can be made coherent. His action-based account also points toward compatibilism: natural determination need not remove freedom unless it deprives the agent of the relevant powers.
key_ideas: Locke’s deflationary account treats actions as bodily motions or mental operations; forbearances are episodes of rest or absence of thought. He does not need every action to be a deliberate doing.
Voluntariness concerns the relation between a volition and an action, whereas freedom concerns the agent’s available powers. Neither condition is sufficient for the other.

The phrase “free will” can be misleading for Locke because a will is a power, not a substance that can possess another power. He redirects the issue to whether a person is free in relation to willing.
Locke’s initial account says the will is determined by the apparent greater good. His later account instead emphasizes uneasiness, while recognizing that people may act against their better judgment.
The doctrine of suspension gives agents a power to delay desire and investigate whether a proposed goal contributes to their genuine good. This helps connect freedom with moral responsibility.
Interpretations differ about whether Locke thinks people are free to will what they will. His revisions, especially the limitation to present actions and ongoing processes, are central to the debate.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke separates several issues often compressed into the phrase “free will”: whether an action is voluntary, whether an agent has the ability to act or refrain, whether a person can suspend desire, and whether the will itself can be free. These distinctions remain useful in debates about responsibility, coercion, weakness of will, and the relationship between causal explanation and human agency.

important_terms.definition: For Locke, a two-way power: an agent is free regarding an action when the agent can perform it if willing to do so and can refrain if willing not to do so.
A power or faculty that directs one’s body or mind toward beginning, continuing, ending, or refraining from an action.
An act in which the mind directs itself toward producing an action or forbearance that it takes to be within its power.
An action or forbearance caused, in the relevant way, by a volition concerning that action; without such a volition, it is involuntary.
A painful or restless condition of body or mind, often arising from the lack of an absent good, that usually determines the will.
The power to delay the fulfillment of a desire in order to examine and weigh it against other considerations.
The view that free will and causal determinism can both be true.

questions_to_think_about: Does an action count as free whenever it follows your choice, or must you also have had genuine alternatives?
Why might Locke distinguish the freedom to act from the freedom to will?
Can uneasiness cause a choice without making the choice involuntary?
Does the ability to suspend desire add a new kind of freedom, or is it one part of freedom already defined?
Why might compatibility between freedom and determination by uneasiness not by itself prove compatibility with causal determinism?

summaries.example: Maya wants to leave a study room, but the door is locked. Her wish is real, and she might even decide to leave, yet she cannot get out. Locke would say that her staying could be voluntary if she chooses to remain, but she is not free to leave because the locked door removes that ability. If the door is unlocked, she can stay or leave according to her decision, so she is free about that action.
summaries.summary: John Locke’s account of freedom asks what people are able to do or refrain from doing according to their minds. He treats both bodily movements and mental activities as actions, and he also discusses forbearances, such as remaining still or not speaking. The will is a power that directs the body or mind. Volition, or willing, is the mind’s direction toward an action it takes to be possible. An action is voluntary when it follows the appropriate volition, while an action can be involuntary when it occurs without such direction. Freedom is not the same as voluntariness. Someone locked in a room might voluntarily stay because they prefer the company inside, but that person is not free to leave. In contrast, a person’s arm might be moved by someone else even though the person is free to raise or lower it. Locke also rejects the question of whether the will is free, because the will is a power and powers are not the kinds of things that possess powers. He instead asks whether a person can be free while willing and whether a person can will whatever that person wills. His answers are complicated by changes between editions of his work. Locke first says that the apparent greater good determines the will. Later, he argues that uneasiness—pain, worry, or the felt lack of something—usually motivates the will. Yet people can suspend a desire, consider its consequences, and compare it with other goals. This ability helps explain responsibility: a person may be blameworthy not simply for having a desire, but for rushing to follow it without examining whether it leads toward genuine happiness. Locke’s account suggests a form of compatibilism, although the entry notes that determination by uneasiness is not automatically the same as causal determinism.
key_ideas: Locke defines freedom through ability: you are free about an action when you can do it if you decide to and can refrain if you decide not to.
Voluntary action and freedom are different. A person may choose to stay in a locked room, but cannot freely leave.
Locke says the will is a power, not a little person inside us. Therefore, asking whether the will itself is free is a confused question.
In an earlier version of his view, Locke says the will follows what seems like the greatest good. In a later version, he says uneasiness usually drives the will.
People sometimes act against what they know is better because a strong immediate feeling pushes them. Locke’s power of suspension gives them a chance to pause and think.
Many interpreters see Locke as leaning toward compatibilism, because he thinks causes do not destroy freedom unless they remove the person’s ability to act as decided.
summaries.why_it_matters: This theory gives us tools for discussing everyday and serious questions about choice. It shows why being pressured, blocked, influenced, or physically moved are not all the same. It also connects freedom with reflection: the ability to pause and examine a desire may be more important than simply having many wishes.

important_terms.definition: Having the power to do something or refrain from doing it according to one’s own decision.
A power of the mind that directs the body or thoughts, such as ordering oneself to speak or remain silent.
The mind’s act of directing an action or stopping an action that it believes is within its power.
An action that happens because of the right kind of choice or direction from the mind.
A feeling of pain, worry, or lack that presses a person toward some change or action.
Pausing a desire so that one can examine it before acting.
The view that freedom can exist even if events have causes that determine what happens.

questions_to_think_about: If someone chooses to stay in a locked room, is staying voluntary, free, both, or neither?
Why might wanting something be different from willing it?
Can pausing before a choice make a person more responsible?
Does being influenced by a feeling mean that a decision was not your own?
Is freedom mainly about having choices, carrying them out, or both?
